chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Rocket Lab Corporation (RKLB, NASDAQ) is the principal listed Western small-launch pure-play — and, as of May 2026, something considerably more complex than that. Founded in Auckland, New Zealand in 2006 by engineer Peter Beck and now headquartered in Long Beach, California, the company operates the only orbital small-launch vehicle in the Western world flying at commercial scale, a rapidly expanding spacecraft and satellite-components manufacturing business, and the most consequential new launch vehicle in active development outside SpaceX. Electron had accumulated 88 total launches by 22 May 2026, making it the most-launched non-SpaceX American launch vehicle — a milestone the company marked on its press release that day after completing its [ninth dedicated mission for Tokyo-based radar satellite operator Synspective](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/05/22/3299998/0/en/Mission-Success-Rocket-Lab-Completes-9th-Electron-Launch-for-Synspective.html).

## Corporate Anatomy

Rocket Lab operates through two reported segments. Launch Services encompasses the Electron small-launch vehicle — which carries payloads of up to 335 kg to low Earth orbit from Launch Complex 1 at Mahia, New Zealand and Launch Complex 2 at Wallops Island, Virginia — alongside Neutron, the medium-lift vehicle in development targeting approximately 13,000 kg to LEO. Space Systems encompasses the Photon spacecraft platform (originally derived from Electron's upper stage and first flown on the CAPSTONE lunar mission for NASA in 2022), plus an assembled portfolio of satellite components acquired since 2020: Sinclair Interplanetary (reaction wheels, April 2020), Advanced Solutions Inc. (flight software, December 2021), Solero Technologies (solar arrays, December 2021), and Planetary Systems Corporation, traded as Plasma (separation systems, October 2021). The SPAC business combination with Vector Acquisition Corporation closed 25 August 2021 at an implied enterprise value of approximately $4.1 billion, putting Beck's vertically integrated franchise onto the public markets three years after Electron's first successful orbital flight.

## The Numbers

Rocket Lab's revenue growth since the SPAC listing has been steep and consistent. Full-year 2025 revenue reached a record $601.8 million — up 38% year-on-year — following $436.2 million in 2024, itself representing 78% annual growth over the $245 million posted in 2023. The compound picture from the post-SPAC baseline is striking.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD) | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | $62M | — |
| 2022 | $211M | +241% |
| 2023 | $245M | +16% |
| 2024 | $436M | +78% |
| 2025 | $602M | +38% |

The company remains pre-profit. Net loss in 2025 was $198.2 million. The [2024 full-year results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250227056608/en/Rocket-Lab-Announces-Full-Year-Fourth-Quarter-2024-Financial-Results-Posts-Record-Revenue-Representing-26-Sequential-Growth-78-Annual-Growth-and-121-Year-on-Year-Quarterly-Growth) showed the Space Systems segment contributed approximately $311 million — roughly 71% of that year's total revenue — against $125 million from Launch Services. Space Systems' dominance of the revenue mix reflects both the Photon platform's traction and the organic growth of the acquired components businesses, which sell into the broader commercial and government satellite supply chain beyond Rocket Lab's own missions. By the end of 2025, the company carried a contract backlog of $1.85 billion, up 73% year-on-year, with the [Q4 2025 and full-year results announcement](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/02/26/3246099/0/en/Rocket-Lab-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results-Posts-Record-Quarterly-Revenue-of-180M-Record-Annual-Revenue-of-602M-Delivering-Annual-Growth-of-38-and-Gro.html) citing record quarterly revenue of $180 million in Q4.

## Customer Base

Electron's customer roster spans civil, commercial, and defence. NASA's CAPSTONE lunar cubesat in 2022 furnished the company's highest-visibility civil mission and validated the Photon bus for deep-space applications. The US Space Force and the broader Department of Defense have become structurally important: Neutron was [on-ramped onto the Space Force's $5.6 billion NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 programme](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-labs-neutron-rocket-on-ramped-to-u-s-space-forces-5-6b-national-security-space-launch-nssl-program/) in March 2025, positioning it to compete for national security launch task orders from FY2026 alongside ULA and SpaceX. In December 2025, the Space Development Agency awarded Rocket Lab an [$816 million prime contract](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/12/19/3208731/0/en/Rocket-Lab-Awarded-816M-Prime-Contract-to-Build-Missile-Defense-Satellite-Constellation-for-U-S-Space-Force.html) to design and build 18 satellites for the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture's Tracking Layer Tranche 3 — the company's single largest programme award to date and a signal that the Space Systems segment is now operating as a prime satellite integrator rather than a components vendor. Commercial customers include Synspective (nine dedicated Electron launches), Capella Space, and Globalstar, which holds a multi-launch agreement.

## Neutron: The Medium-Launch Bet

Neutron is the strategic inflection point that either transforms Rocket Lab from a small-launch specialist into a Falcon 9-class competitor or exposes the difficulty of developing a new medium-lift vehicle from a standing start. The vehicle is a partially reusable, carbon-composite rocket targeting approximately 13 metric tons to LEO — designed to return its first stage for landing rather than expendable flight, and explicitly positioned as the principal Western commercial alternative to the Falcon 9. The first launch, originally targeted for 2025, [slipped to Q4 2026](https://spacenews.com/rocket-lab-delays-first-neutron-launch-to-2026/) after an unanticipated failure during qualification testing of the first-stage propellant tank in early 2026. Development milestones confirmed through the snapshot date include qualification of the "Hungry Hippo" clamshell fairing, delivery of that fairing to the Virginia Assembly and Integration Complex, and completion of thrust-structure qualification. The Archimedes engine remains in qualification. Beck's own framing of Neutron's schedule has consistently acknowledged risk: "complexity of a new launch vehicle which could impact current best estimate of a targeted timeline for first launch."

## The Central Question

The picture at the snapshot date is of a company that has executed with unusual consistency on the small-launch side — 88 missions, industry-leading annual cadence of 21 flights in 2025, and a Space Systems segment whose scale now dwarfs its launch revenue — while carrying the still-unresolved risk of a medium-launch programme whose schedule has slipped once and whose first-stage propulsion and tank systems have not yet achieved full qualification. Rocket Lab is the most credible listed alternative to SpaceX in both launch services and vertically integrated spacecraft manufacturing. The dossier examines, in turn, whether Neutron can close the gap, what the Space Systems acquisition arc has actually built, and where the competitive lines between Rocket Lab and SpaceX are drawn and where they run in parallel.

chapters.title: From the 2006 New Zealand founding through Electron, the 2021 SPAC, and Neutron
chapters.body:
## A Workshop in Wellington, a Rocket in Mahia

Peter Beck did not arrive at rocketry through a conventional path. The New Zealand engineer — largely self-taught, with formative years spent at the government-backed Industrial Research Limited in Wellington — founded Rocket Lab in 2006 with a conviction that was then contrarian: that the small satellite market would eventually require its own dedicated, low-cost launch infrastructure, not a secondary berth on large rockets designed for heavier payloads. Beck was in his mid-twenties. The idea attracted little immediate institutional capital, and the company's early years were defined by bootstrap engineering in Auckland rather than Sand Hill Road fundraising rounds.

The core insight was architectural. Where the incumbent launch industry had been built around maximising payload mass — Atlas V, Ariane 5, the Proton — Beck argued the emerging commercial small satellite market would create demand for frequent, dedicated rideshare at far lower price points. The vehicle he designed around that thesis was Electron: a two-stage carbon-composite rocket powered by a cluster of nine Rutherford engines at first stage, with a single Rutherford vacuum variant at second. The Rutherford was itself a signal of Beck's engineering ambition — a liquid bipropellant engine manufactured predominantly via additive manufacturing (3D printing), a first for a production orbital rocket engine.

Rocket Lab established [Launch Complex 1](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/launch/launch-complex-1/) on the Māhia Peninsula on New Zealand's North Island, a private orbital launch site whose geography — a narrow promontory jutting into open ocean — offered the azimuth flexibility needed to serve a broad range of low Earth orbit inclinations. The facility required negotiating new regulatory frameworks with the New Zealand government; the country ultimately passed the Outer Space and High-altitude Activities Act in 2017, giving Rocket Lab the first privately-operated orbital launch site in the Southern Hemisphere.

## Electron's Debut and the Commercial Era

The path to first orbital flight was not clean. Rocket Lab's first Electron test vehicle, "It's a Test," reached space in May 2017 but failed to reach orbit owing to a ground systems communications fault that triggered a range safety termination. A second test flight, "Still Testing," achieved orbit in January 2018 — the milestone that opened the commercial era. The company's first commercial launch, "It's Business Time," followed in November 2018, carrying payloads for Spire Global, GeoOptics, and IRVINE CubeSat STEM Programme. The vehicle's advertised payload capacity of 300 kilograms to a 500-kilometre sun-synchronous orbit, at a then-listed price of approximately $7.5 million per dedicated mission, positioned Electron squarely at the emerging small satellite operator market.

The years from 2018 through 2020 were characterised by cadence building. Rocket Lab conducted six Electron missions in 2019 and seven in 2020 — a launch rate that no other dedicated small-launch vehicle operator matched in that period. The customer manifest diversified across commercial imaging (Synspective, Capella Space), maritime tracking (Spire), and US government payloads, including early work for the National Reconnaissance Office under its rapid-acquisition NROL programmes. Beck relocated the company's corporate headquarters to Long Beach, California, in proximity to the US aerospace and defence contracting infrastructure, while preserving full New Zealand manufacturing and launch operations.

In 2020, Rocket Lab opened a second launch facility: [Launch Complex 2](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/launch/launch-complex-2/) at the Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport at NASA's Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia, oriented primarily toward US government missions requiring domestically-launched vehicles. The dual-site infrastructure — Southern Hemisphere commercial plus US East Coast government — became a material competitive differentiator as US Space Force and intelligence community customers began directing dedicated launch procurements.

## The SPAC Combination

Rocket Lab entered 2021 as a private company with disclosed funding approaching $290 million across multiple rounds from investors including Bessemer Venture Partners, DCVC (Data Collective), Khosla Ventures, and Greenspring Associates. The decision to pursue a public listing via SPAC merger resulted in the August 25, 2021 close of Rocket Lab's business combination with [Vector Acquisition Corporation](https://investors.rocketlabusa.com/), delivering approximately $750 million in gross proceeds. Rocket Lab's shares began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker RKLB the same day.

The public listing crystallised a strategic posture that Beck had been articulating since at least 2019: Rocket Lab was not simply a launch provider but a vertically integrated space company — one that could manufacture spacecraft, supply subsystems, and operate on-orbit platforms, not merely place payloads into orbit. The SPAC proceeds were earmarked explicitly for two purposes: scaling Electron cadence and funding development of Neutron, the medium-class launch vehicle Beck had announced in March 2021 as Rocket Lab's answer to the heavier end of the commercial satellite market.

## The Acquisition Arc

The Space Systems build-out had begun ahead of the SPAC close. In April 2020, Rocket Lab acquired [Sinclair Interplanetary](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/space-systems/), the Toronto-based manufacturer of small spacecraft reaction wheels and other attitude-control components whose products had flown on hundreds of small satellites. The acquisition gave Rocket Lab direct access to the component supply chain its own Photon spacecraft platform required — and, more importantly, a revenue stream from third-party satellite operators who sourced Sinclair hardware independently of any Rocket Lab launch relationship.

Three further acquisitions followed in the second half of 2021, executed in rapid succession after the SPAC close delivered liquidity. In October 2021, Rocket Lab acquired Plasma, a New Zealand-based developer of Hall-effect electric propulsion thrusters used in small satellite station-keeping and orbit-raising. In December 2021, it acquired Advanced Solutions Inc. (ASI), a Colorado-based spacecraft software and mission simulation business, and separately acquired Solero Technologies, a provider of solar panels and power systems for small satellites. The four acquisitions together constituted a deliberate vertical integration strategy: Rocket Lab could now offer a customer a reaction-wheel attitude control system (Sinclair), solar power generation (Solero), electric propulsion (Plasma), spacecraft software (ASI), and a complete Photon spacecraft bus — before the customer's satellite ever reached the Electron manifest.

The financial effect was substantial. By 2024, Space Systems contributed approximately 70 to 75 percent of total revenue — inverting the original launch-services identity that had defined the company's public profile. The company remained pre-profit through 2024, with operating losses sustained by Neutron development and the integration costs of acquired businesses.

## Neutron and the Unfinished Timetable

Beck announced Neutron in March 2021, targeting the 13,000-kilogram-to-low-Earth-orbit class — a vehicle explicitly designed to compete with the SpaceX Falcon 9 on commercial constellation replenishment, national security medium launch, and eventual crewed spaceflight. The architecture diverged sharply from Electron: a reusable first stage with a "returning to Earth" direct-landing profile, a carbon-composite structure, and the Archimedes engine — a new development using liquid oxygen and methane propellants, designed for reusability from the outset.

The original first-launch target of 2024 slipped. Beck acknowledged in quarterly earnings commentary through 2024 and 2025 that the development programme had encountered timeline pressure, with the revised public target moving to late 2025 and subsequently into 2026. The Archimedes engine development — involving first firings and a test campaign at Rocket Lab's Stennis Space Center facilities in Mississippi — represented the programme's critical path item. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Neutron had not yet flown.

The slippages did not alter Beck's public framing of Neutron's strategic logic. The medium launch market, he argued consistently, remained structurally underserved outside SpaceX, and Neutron's reusable architecture was positioned to address that gap at competitive economics. Whether the vehicle could achieve first launch within a commercially meaningful window — before the market consolidated further around SpaceX's Falcon 9 manifest — remained the central unresolved question confronting the company's long-term trajectory.

chapters.title: Electron, Neutron, Photon, and the Space Systems components portfolio
chapters.body:
## Two Rockets, One Platform, a Portfolio of Components

The architecture Peter Beck settled on as Rocket Lab matured was not the architecture of a launch company that happened to make satellites. It was the architecture of a company that understood launch as the entry credential and spacecraft as the compounding asset. The business reorganised around two principal reporting segments: Launch Services, anchored by Electron and its growing cadence of missions, and Space Systems, a deliberately assembled portfolio of spacecraft hardware, propulsion, and software capabilities. By 2024, Space Systems accounted for approximately 70 to 75 percent of revenue. That asymmetry is the consequence of design, not drift.

## Electron: The Workhorse in Orbit

Electron is the vehicle that gave Rocket Lab its standing in the industry. A two-stage carbon-composite liquid-fuelled rocket powered by the company's own Rutherford engine — itself notable for being the first electric-pump-fed engine to reach orbit — Electron lifts approximately 335 kilograms to low Earth orbit on a dedicated mission. It operates from [Launch Complex 1 at Mahia Peninsula, New Zealand](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/launch/launch-sites/), and from [Launch Complex 2 at Wallops Island, Virginia](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/launch/launch-sites/), giving Rocket Lab the only private launch operator with active pads on two continents.

The vehicle entered commercial service in 2018 and by end-2025 had surpassed 50 missions — a record unmatched by any other Western small-launch competitor.

The competitive landscape Electron occupies is defined partly by what it is not. The vehicle does not compete with SpaceX's Falcon 9 on total payload mass; it is not designed to. Where Electron's 335-kilogram capacity constrains it relative to a Falcon 9 rideshare manifest, it simultaneously enables something rideshare cannot: a dedicated orbital insertion into a customer-specified inclination, at a customer-specified time, with no schedule dependency on another operator's primary payload. For small satellite operators — commercial Earth-observation companies, government science missions, defence reconnaissance assets — that scheduling certainty has commercial value that rideshare pricing cannot always replicate.

| Vehicle | Payload to LEO | Class | Reuse |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron (Rocket Lab) | ~335 kg | Small | Partial (recovery trials) |
| Falcon 9 (SpaceX) | ~22,800 kg | Medium-heavy | Yes (first stage) |
| Firefly Alpha | ~1,000 kg | Small | No |
| Vulcan Centaur (ULA) | ~27,200 kg | Heavy | No |

Rocket Lab initiated booster recovery trials for Electron beginning in 2020, successfully capturing a returning first stage with a helicopter during an [April 2022 mission](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/updates/rocket-lab-completes-historic-mid-air-helicopter-capture-of-electron-rocket-returning-from-space/) before proceeding with ocean recovery for subsequent missions. The programme remained developmental through the snapshot period: Rocket Lab was not routinely reflying Electron first stages at the same cadence SpaceX had achieved with Falcon 9, but the company had demonstrated the core recovery mechanics and accumulated hardware for inspection.

Principal customers through the period included [Synspective](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/missions/), the Japanese synthetic-aperture radar operator; [Capella Space](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/missions/), the US commercial SAR provider; [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/) for multiple science missions; the US Space Force and broader Department of Defense for undisclosed reconnaissance payloads; and [Globalstar](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/updates/), under a multi-launch agreement for the satellite operator's constellation maintenance. The DoD relationship deepened through the period as Space Force and related agencies sought access to dedicated small-launch capacity with US-domiciled operational control.

## Neutron: The Competitive Escalation

Rocket Lab announced Neutron publicly in March 2021 as an explicit declaration of intent to enter the medium-launch market — the segment supporting large constellation replenishment, where SpaceX's Falcon 9 dominates.

> "Neutron isn't just another rocket. It's a rocket designed from the start to be reused, and designed from the start to be built at a cost structure that makes it commercially viable against the incumbents."

The programme required construction of new manufacturing infrastructure in Middle River, Maryland, and a dedicated launch pad at Wallops Island.

## Photon and the Spacecraft Platform

Between the two launch vehicles sits the Photon spacecraft platform — the product that most clearly expresses Rocket Lab's vertical-integration logic. Photon originated as the Electron kick stage, a small propulsion module sitting above the main payload to perform final orbital insertion manoeuvres. Over successive iterations the platform was developed into a full spacecraft bus: attitude control, power management, communications, and propulsion integrated into a structure that could support commercial remote sensing payloads, government science instruments, or broader mission architectures.

Photon's capability was validated by the 2022 CAPSTONE lunar mission for NASA, which demonstrated the platform's ability to operate beyond Earth orbit.

## Space Systems: The Acquisition Architecture

The Space Systems segment's revenue dominance — roughly three-quarters of total 2024 revenue — reflects a deliberate aggregation of satellite component and subsystem manufacturers acquired between 2020 and 2021.

The 2020–2022 acquisition arc — Sinclair Interplanetary (reaction wheels), plasma propulsion (Hall-effect thrusters), ASI (flight software), and Solero (solar arrays) — gave Rocket Lab the ability to supply attitude control, electric propulsion, power generation, and software from a single vendor. Beck's stated objective was to compress the component supply chain such that Rocket Lab could manufacture complete spacecraft for customers who did not want to assemble them from parts, while also supplying parts to operators who preferred to build their own.

The two segments — a launch business defined by Electron's accumulated flight record and Neutron's development trajectory, and a space systems business built from acquired component manufacturers and the Photon platform — formed the structural logic that Rocket Lab would carry into the Neutron launch era.

chapters.title: $437M revenue, operating losses, and the Neutron capex trajectory
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Arc Rebuilt From Scratch

The August 2021 SPAC close marked a baseline: $62 million in annual revenue. Three fiscal years later, that figure had grown to $436.2 million — a compound annual growth rate of roughly 91 percent. The trajectory is, by any standard of the space industry, extraordinary. The losses are proportionally large, the capital structure is now substantially leveraged, and the largest item on the forward expense ledger is a rocket that has not yet flown.

Understanding the financial architecture of Rocket Lab requires separating two businesses that happen to share a balance sheet: a small-launch franchise anchored by the Electron rocket, and a space-systems integrator assembled largely through acquisition. The former has grown steadily; the latter has scaled explosively. Together they have produced a revenue curve that few listed aerospace companies have matched in a comparable time window — and an operating-loss series that demands equal scrutiny.

## The Segment Shift: Space Systems Takes Command

The clearest financial story in Rocket Lab's post-SPAC record is the inversion of its segment mix. At the 2021 baseline, Launch Services contributed roughly $39 million of the $62 million total, with the nascent Space Systems unit accounting for the remaining $23 million. By 2022 that relationship had flipped decisively.

| Fiscal Year | Launch Services | Space Systems | Total Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | ~$39.0M | ~$23.3M | $62.2M |
| 2022 | $60.7M | $150.3M | $211.0M |
| 2023 | $71.9M | $172.7M | $244.6M |
| 2024 | $125.4M | $310.8M | $436.2M |

Sources: [Rocket Lab 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001819994](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001819994&type=10-K); [Rocket Lab Q4 2024 earnings press release](https://www.rocketlabusa.com/investors/)

The Space Systems explosion in 2022 — from $23 million to $150 million in a single year — reflected the consolidation of acquisitions completed in 2020–2021, creating what management described as a "constellation-in-a-box" capability.

By fiscal year 2024, Space Systems represented 71 percent of total revenue at $310.8 million, growing 80 percent year-over-year. Launch Services — encompassing Electron missions from both the New Zealand Launch Complex 1 at Māhia and the Virginia Launch Complex 2 at Wallops — delivered $125.4 million, up 74 percent on the prior year, reflecting higher launch cadence and a rising average selling price per mission as the manifest has tilted toward more capable payloads and government customers.

## Operating Losses: The Cost of Structural Ambition

Revenue growth of this magnitude has not converted to positive operating income. Rocket Lab posted an operating loss of $135.2 million in 2022, widening to $177.9 million in 2023 and to $189.8 million in 2024 — representing a roughly 40 percent cumulative expansion of losses even as revenue grew 107 percent over the same two-year span. The gross margin trajectory, however, tells a more encouraging internal story: the company reported $116.1 million in gross profit in 2024 against $436.2 million in revenue, a gross margin of 26.6 percent. The operating loss therefore reflects the cost structure sitting above the gross line.

Research and development expenditure reached $174.4 million in fiscal 2024, and selling, general and administrative costs consumed a further $131.6 million — together accounting for more than $305 million in operating expense against $116 million of gross profit. The predominant driver of the R&D line is Neutron. Management has not disclosed a precise quarterly allocation of Neutron engineering spend within the R&D figure, but on the Q4 2024 earnings call Peter Beck confirmed cumulative programme spend on Neutron through year-end 2024 of approximately $200 million across both capitalised and expensed components. The forward trajectory, per updated guidance from chief financial officer Adam Spice, calls for cumulative Neutron programme expenditure of approximately $360 million through the end of 2025.

For 2024's first quarter, the operating loss ran at $43.1 million. By Q1 2025, that quarterly run-rate had increased to $59.2 million, consistent with the Neutron capex ramp described below. On an annualised basis, the Q1 2025 figure would imply operating losses in the range of $235 million for 2025 in total — though the company has guided for improving unit economics as Electron launch cadence rises.

## The SPAC Windfall and Its Dissipation

The August 2021 SPAC merger delivered approximately $777 million in gross proceeds, comprising roughly $470 million in PIPE commitments and $320 million from the Vector trust account. Cash and equivalents at December 31, 2021 stood at $691.0 million. That reserve funded two full years of operations, acquisitions, and capital expenditure before the company returned to the capital markets.

By year-end 2022 cash had fallen to $242.5 million as the company absorbed the acquisition costs and integration expenses of the late-2021 deal cluster. By year-end 2023, with no material equity or debt raise in the intervening period, cash had declined further to $162.5 million — a level that, measured against a quarterly operating cash burn exceeding $40 million, had become uncomfortably thin.

The February 2024 convertible senior notes offering resolved that constraint, but at a cost that materially reshaped the capital structure.

## The February 2024 Convertible Notes

Rocket Lab priced $355.0 million in aggregate principal of 4.250% Convertible Senior Notes due February 1, 2029 in February 2024. The offering was upsized twice from an initial $275 million indication, reflecting strong institutional demand. [BusinessWire, February 7, 2024](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240207769898/en/Rocket-Lab-Announces-Closing-of-Upsized-Offering-of-$355-Million-Convertible-Senior-Notes). The notes carry a coupon payable semi-annually and an initial conversion price of approximately $5.13 per share, representing roughly 195.1 shares per $1,000 principal — a structure that creates meaningful dilution risk if the stock sustains levels above that threshold.

The company simultaneously executed capped call transactions at a cost of $43.2 million, designed to economically offset dilution up to a cap price above the conversion price. Net proceeds to Rocket Lab after capped calls and underwriting fees were approximately $300.3 million.

The equipment lending relationship with Trinity Capital was also expanded, with a $120 million facility announced in February 2024 to finance manufacturing equipment and test infrastructure, [Trinity Capital press release, February 2024](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/trinity-capital-inc-provides-120-million-equipment-financing-to-rocket-lab-302066342.html), replacing an earlier facility of roughly $100 million.

The combined effect was a near-tripling of total debt — from $176.7 million at year-end 2023 to $468.4 million at year-end 2024 — and a rebuilding of the cash position to $271.0 million. Including $208.6 million in short-term marketable securities, total liquidity at December 31, 2024 was approximately $484 million.

## Neutron's Capital Demands and the Capex Ramp

The total company capital expenditure figure is the most visible proxy for Neutron construction activity. Capex ran at $54.7 million in fiscal 2023, rising to $67.1 million in fiscal 2024 — a 23 percent increase that understate the acceleration visible in individual quarters. Q1 2025 capex registered $28.7 million against Q1 2024's $19.2 million, a 49 percent year-over-year step-up reflecting the inauguration of major physical infrastructure at the company's Neutron production facility in Wallops Island, Virginia.

The programme encompasses a new large-structure composites manufacturing building, a dedicated engine test stand at NASA Stennis Space Center for the Archimedes engine, and the associated tooling for a rocket with a gross liftoff mass that dwarfs Electron by roughly an order of magnitude.

Management has consistently declined to provide a standalone annual Neutron capex figure within the quarterly filings, characterising the programme expenditure as embedded within both the capital expenditure line and the R&D expense line. The cumulative disclosure — $200 million through end-2024, approximately $360 million through end-2025 — implies roughly $160 million in incremental combined programme spend during 2025 alone, consistent with the sharp Q1 2025 capex upswing.

## 2025 Trajectory: Growth Confirmed, Profitability Deferred

Quarterly revenue of $122.6 million in Q1 2025 represented 32 percent growth over the year-earlier quarter and implied an annualised run rate exceeding $490 million. Management guided Q2 2025 revenue to $130–$140 million. The backlog at year-end 2024 stood at $1.07 billion — $386 million attributable to launch services and $681 million to space systems — providing multi-quarter forward visibility unusual for a company of Rocket Lab's scale.

> "We are seeing strong, continued demand across both our launch and space systems businesses, and our backlog is at record levels," Beck told analysts on the Q4 2024 call, adding that the pipeline reflected "customers increasingly choosing Rocket Lab as a complete mission provider rather than just a launch service." [Rocket Lab Q4 2024 earnings call, February 2025]

The tension between that demand signal and the widening loss rate through 2024 reflects precisely the Neutron investment horizon. The question the financial record poses is straightforward: Rocket Lab has demonstrated that the Space Systems segment can scale, that Electron can achieve launch cadence sufficient to grow launch revenue materially, and that the capital markets are willing to fund the gap. What it has not yet demonstrated is a path to operating profitability that does not depend on Neutron's commercial success — a vehicle that, as of the snapshot date, remained in development with first launch targeted in 2025 or 2026.

chapters.title: Post-SPAC quarters through the Neutron development trajectory
chapters.body:
## The Post-SPAC Baseline

The August 2021 SPAC close delivered $777 million in gross proceeds, deployed across two tracks: Electron cadence expansion and Neutron clean-sheet development. Acquisitions straddling the close had already begun assembling what Beck described as a vertically integrated space-systems business.

## The Acquisition Arc and Space Systems Scaling

January 2022 brought the close of SolAero Technologies at approximately $80 million, addressing a supply-chain vulnerability: reliable, flight-qualified solar power generation. The SolAero deal completed the component catalogue — attitude control, separation systems, power generation, mission software, propulsion — that could flow into third-party programmes or integrate into Photon.

Revenue tripled in 2022 as acquired businesses contributed full-year revenue. The 2023 fiscal year marked transition toward organic growth, with the 2024 acceleration — $437 million, up 78 percent — confirming the Space Systems ramp. See **Financial Deep Dive** for detailed segment breakouts.

## Electron: Cadence as Industrial Proof Point

The programme crossed 30 cumulative missions by end-2022, exceeded 40 by 2023, and surpassed 50 through 2025. The May 2022 mid-air helicopter catch demonstrated that Rocket Lab's unconventional recovery architecture was executable in practice.

## Neutron: Development Trajectory and Slippage

The design specification that emerged through earnings cycles called for a carbon-composite first stage powered by nine Archimedes LOX/methane engines, targeting approximately 13,000 kilograms to LEO. The development timeline slipped from the original 2024 target to late 2025, then toward 2026:

> "Neutron is the hardest thing we have ever undertaken. We are building a new engine and a new vehicle class simultaneously, and we are not going to shortcut that process to hit an arbitrary date."

As of the snapshot date, Neutron had not reached its inaugural launch. Beck's dual role as founder, chairman, and chief executive concentrated Neutron's pace and strategic direction at a single authority.

chapters.title: Peter Beck, Adam Spice CFO, segment leadership, and the post-SPAC board
chapters.body:
## The Man from Invercargill

Peter Beck did not follow the canonical aerospace path. There was no aerospace engineering degree, no graduate fellowship at a national laboratory, no early posting at a legacy prime contractor. Beck grew up in Invercargill, at the southern tip of New Zealand's South Island, the son of a museum director and gemologist and a teacher. He enrolled as a tool-and-die-maker apprentice at Fisher & Paykel in 1995, and it was there — in the company workshops at night, after hours — that he began teaching himself rocket propulsion by doing it.

The formal scientific grounding came later, at [Industrial Research Limited](https://www.sciencelearn.org.nz/resources/398-sir-peter-beck), the New Zealand government research organisation, where Beck worked from 2001 to 2006 on smart materials, composites and superconductors. It was at IRL that he encountered Stephen Tindall, who would become one of Rocket Lab's earliest investors. In 2006 Beck accompanied his wife on a work trip to the United States and turned the journey into what he later called a "rocket pilgrimage" — driving across the country to meet Ky Michaelson, a veteran rocketeer known as "Rocketman," and calling in at NASA, Lockheed Martin, and a constellation of US defence contractors. He returned to New Zealand and founded Rocket Lab later that year.

The résumé reads as improbable, and Beck has acknowledged as much. "Half of my brain is the go-getter entrepreneur," he told Space.com in April 2024. "The other half of my brain is the engineer realist." The tension between those two halves has defined his leadership style through two decades of company building — the entrepreneur who set audacious targets, and the engineer who understood precisely how hard meeting them would be.

## Chairman and CEO: The Dual-Role Structure

Beck was appointed Chairman of the Board in May 2021, three months before the August SPAC close. The dual CEO-Chairman structure was a deliberate signal of founder continuity — Beck's concentrated authority serving as the governance equivalent of a long-dated call option on the company's Neutron ambition.

Critics of dual CEO-Chairman structures cite accountability gaps and reduced board independence. Rocket Lab mitigated this through a Lead Independent Director designation held from the company's public listing by Merline Saintil, and through the installation of fully independent audit and compensation committees. Beck himself offered little apology for the structure. "This industry and the public markets are all about execution," he said on the day of Rocket Lab's NASDAQ debut in August 2021. "The wheat from the chaff will get separated very, very quickly here."

In June 2024, the New Zealand government formalised what the space industry had long recognised: Beck was appointed a Knight Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit — Sir Peter Beck KNZM — for services to the aerospace industry, business and education. The ceremony was, by disposition, a minor distraction. Rocket Lab by that point employed roughly 1,800 people across Long Beach, California, Auckland, and multiple other facilities, and was pressing through the most technically demanding phase of Neutron development.

Beck's public persona has been shaped as much by memorable theatrics as by engineering milestone. In March 2021, announcing the Neutron medium-lift programme — a direct challenge to the doctrine he had spent years articulating about the supremacy of dedicated small launch — he put a Rocket Lab hat into a blender and consumed the result on camera. "For the avoidance of all doubt," he said, visibly suppressing a grimace, "this hat is not tasty." The stunt embedded a piece of company lore while making a serious strategic point: Beck was reversing a stated position because the market had changed, and he was doing so publicly and with self-deprecation intact.

## Adam Spice: The Semiconductor-Trained CFO

[Adam Spice](https://2023.satelliteinnovation.com/speakers/adam-spice/) joined Rocket Lab as Chief Financial Officer in May 2018, more than three years before the SPAC listing. His retention through the transaction and into the post-public period provided a rare form of institutional continuity: the CFO who had already done the pre-public financial architecture was the same CFO who explained the capital structure to investors on day one.

Spice's background was semiconductor and fabless chip, not aerospace. At MaxLinear (2010–2018), he presided over revenue growth from approximately $70 million to $421 million and oversaw more than 50 strategic acquisitions — M&A experience directly relevant to assembling Rocket Lab's Space Systems segment. He holds a BBA from Brigham Young University and an MBA from the University of Texas at Austin.

In quarterly earnings presentations, Spice has handled the financial narrative of a company operating two segments with sharply different economic profiles — a launch business whose per-mission revenue is high but whose manufacturing costs are front-loaded, and a space systems business that throws off contract revenue at higher gross margins but requires sustained engineering investment. His presentation of the path toward adjusted EBITDA breakeven, alongside Beck's technical commentary, has been the consistent format through which Rocket Lab has communicated its financial trajectory to public markets.

## Operational Leadership

The day-to-day execution of Rocket Lab's programmes runs through Frank Klein, who serves as Chief Operating Officer. Klein's portfolio spans the Electron production cadence at the Huntington Beach and Auckland facilities, the Neutron development programme at Wallops Island, and the space systems manufacturing operations assembled through the acquisition arc. The scaling demands are substantial: sustaining Electron's launch rate, running Neutron development in parallel, and integrating multiple acquired engineering cultures into a single operational system.

Brian Rogers, carrying the dual title of Senior Vice President of Global Launch Services and Chief Revenue Officer, leads the commercial organisation. Rogers manages the customer relationships that underpin the launch backlog — a portfolio spanning commercial satellite operators, civil space agencies, and US national security customers including the Space Force. The National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 2 award, announced in 2023, placed Rocket Lab among five certified providers eligible for Defence Department launch contracts alongside SpaceX, ULA, and others — a competitive designation that expanded the addressable market for both Electron and, prospectively, Neutron.

## Board Architecture: From Venture to Establishment

The board assembled at the August 2021 SPAC closing reflected the company's fundraising history as much as its strategic ambitions. The initial post-merger roster paired Beck as Chairman with venture capital representatives who had backed the company through its private phase: [David Cowan](https://www.bvp.com/wish-i-knew/peter-beck) of Bessemer Venture Partners, Matt Ocko of DCVC, and Sven Strohband of Khosla Ventures. Alex Slusky, founder of Vector Capital and chairman of Vector Acquisition Corporation — the SPAC vehicle itself — joined as a director, bringing technology equity and buyout governance perspective. Michael Griffin, the former NASA Administrator and Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, had joined the board in August 2020, pre-SPAC, providing a Washington defence establishment connection that anticipated the company's growing national security revenue.

The composition was calibrated for the transition moment: venture credibility for growth investors, defence establishment credibility for government customers, and a SPAC sponsor with aligned financial incentives. Merline Saintil, a technology executive with career stops at Intuit, Yahoo!, PayPal, Adobe, Joyent, and Sun Microsystems, was appointed Lead Independent Director and brought silicon-valley operational depth to the governance structure.

The board evolved materially through the post-SPAC period as the company's identity shifted from venture-backed startup to defence-adjacent industrial. David Cowan resigned in March 2023. Dr. Edward Frank, a former Apple Vice President of Macintosh Hardware Systems Engineering and Corporate Vice President of R&D at Broadcom, joined in September 2022, taking the Compensation Committee chair. In November 2023, [Lieutenant General Nina Armagno](https://spacenews.com/retired-space-force-lt-gen-armagno-joins-rocket-labs-board-of-directors/) (USAF, retired) was appointed to the board — a highly specific hire. Armagno was the first female general officer commissioned into the United States Space Force, had commanded both the 30th and 45th Space Wings at Vandenberg and Cape Canaveral, and served as the Space Force's inaugural Director of Staff. Her addition brought direct operational familiarity with commercial launch integration, range management, and the procurement priorities of the organisation that Rocket Lab was increasingly dependent upon for contract revenue.

Kenneth Possenriede, who had served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Lockheed Martin from February 2019 through his retirement in August 2021 — a 35-year Lockheed career spanning programme management, aeronautics finance, and corporate CFO — joined the Rocket Lab board in August 2024. His presence as the Audit Committee's principal financial expert, and his institutional knowledge of large-programme cost management, addressed the board's oversight needs as Neutron's development cost and schedule complexity deepened.

Sven Strohband did not stand for re-election at the 2024 Annual Meeting of Stockholders, concluding eleven years of board service. Michael Griffin retired from the board in September 2024. Matt Ocko submitted a written resignation effective November 30, 2025.

## The Board at Snapshot

By May 2026, the seven-member board seated at Rocket Lab's governance table bore little resemblance to the venture-weighted roster of the SPAC era. Peter Beck remained Chairman and CEO, the sole continuous thread from founding to public maturity. Merline Saintil held the Lead Independent Director role, mitigating the governance optics of the dual CEO-Chairman structure. Armagno provided Space Force and range credibility. Possenriede brought Lockheed-scale programme finance experience. Frank contributed deep technology and compensation governance. Olson anchored audit oversight. Slusky maintained continuity from the SPAC sponsor relationship.

The transformation of the board from a VC-dominated startup governance body to a defence-and-aerospace-weighted public company structure was, in its own way, a proxy for the strategic transition Rocket Lab itself was navigating — from a small-launch venture funded by Silicon Valley, to an integrated space industrial whose largest growth lever was Neutron and whose most consequential customers wore uniforms.

> "What we are really focused on here is building an end-to-end space company," Beck told Bloomberg. "Being almost completely vertically integrated means the team has diagnosed and resolved issues rapidly — we don't have to rely on third parties."

The governance apparatus assembled by 2026 was built, at least in theory, to hold him accountable for delivering on that proposition.

---

*Sources: [Peter Beck biography — Science Learning Hub NZ](https://www.sciencelearn.org.nz/resources/398-sir-peter-beck); [Adam Spice profile — Satellite Innovation 2023](https://2023.satelliteinnovation.com/speakers/adam-spice/); [MAXLINEAR Form 8-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001288469/000128846918000011/a2018-04x02exhibit991.htm); [Vector Acquisition Corp Form 425, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001819994/000121390021021742/ea139565-425_vectoracq.htm); [Rocket Lab DEF 14A FY2024, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001819994/000095017024047569/rklb-20240424.htm); [Nina Armagno appointment — SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/retired-space-force-lt-gen-armagno-joins-rocket-labs-board-of-directors/); [Michael Griffin joins board — SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/michael-griffin-joins-rocket-lab-board-of-directors/); [Lockheed CFO joins board — StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/RKLB/former-lockheed-martin-chief-financial-officer-joins-rocket-lab-kx69r85ho4nl.html); [Peter Beck on SPAC debut — TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2021/08/25/peter-beck-on-rocket-labs-public-listing-debut-space-spacs-and-the-neutron-rocket/); [Beck knighthood — Orbital Today](https://orbitaltoday.com/2024/06/05/humbled-and-honoured-rocket-lab-ceo-peter-beck-becomes-the-knight/); [Beck interview April 2024 — Space.com](https://www.space.com/rocket-lab-peter-beck-interview-april-2024); [Beck vertical integration — Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/audio/2025-09-23/tech-disruptors-rocket-lab-s-ceo-on-end-to-end-space-solutions)*

chapters.title: NASA, US Space Force, commercial satellite operators, and the propellant-and-components supply
chapters.body:
Rocket Lab's customer ledger, read in aggregate by early 2026, told the story of a company that had crossed from niche smallsat launcher into something harder to categorise: part government prime contractor, part commercial spacecraft manufacturer, and part critical supplier to the broader Western space industrial base. The transition was not accidental. Peter Beck had from the outset argued that a single-revenue-stream launch company was a fragile organism; the acquisitions and contract wins of the post-SPAC years were the deliberate working-out of that thesis.

## NASA: Science Missions and the Solar Supply Chain

The most visible NASA relationship was CAPSTONE. In February 2020, [NASA selected Rocket Lab](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-contract-to-launch-cubesat-to-moon-from-virginia/) to launch the 55-pound CubeSat to a near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon at a contract value of $9.95 million. The June 2022 launch demonstrated Photon's capability for trans-lunar injection — the most demanding mission the platform had attempted.

The deeper NASA relationship ran through Albuquerque, New Mexico. When Rocket Lab closed its acquisition of SolAero Holdings for $80 million in January 2022, it absorbed one of only two US manufacturers of space-grade compound-semiconductor solar cells. [SolAero's technology](https://techcrunch.com/2022/01/18/rocket-lab-acquires-solaero-holdings-for-80m-to-boost-space-solar-cell-production/) had already powered the Parker Solar Probe, the Mars InSight lander, and multiple Cygnus cargo resupply missions to the International Space Station. The 154,696-square-foot Albuquerque facility subsequently won a contract to supply the Solar Power Modules for NASA's Gateway lunar space station, a component of the Artemis programme. Recognising SolAero's strategic importance to domestic supply security, the Department of Commerce in 2024 [awarded Rocket Lab up to $23.9 million](https://www.nist.gov/chips/rocket-lab-new-mexico-albuquerque) in direct funding under the CHIPS and Science Act to modernise the Albuquerque plant and expand production capacity by fifty per cent.

## From Prime to Warfighter: The US Space Force Franchise

The contract that changed the market's perception of Rocket Lab arrived in January 2024. The Space Development Agency awarded Rocket Lab National Security LLC a $515 million Other Transaction Authority agreement to [build and operate eighteen Beta-variant satellites](https://defensescoop.com/2024/01/08/rocket-lab-sda-tranche-2-beta-award/) for the Tranche 2 Transport Layer, the data-relay backbone of the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture. The award was the company's first as a defence prime — a distinction Beck moved quickly to emphasise on subsequent earnings calls. The satellites, operating in two orbital planes of nine each, carried a launch-no-later-than date of July 2027.

The SDA relationship deepened further in December 2025, when Rocket Lab was awarded an $816 million OTA to [build a missile-defence satellite constellation](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-awarded-816m-prime-contract-to-build-missile-defense-satellite-constellation-for-u-s-space-force/) for the Tranche 3 Tracking Layer. The combined value of Rocket Lab's SDA work had, within roughly two years, grown to more than $1.3 billion.

Alongside the space systems contracts, the launch manifest carried its own national security flavour. In April 2024, the Space Force and the Defense Innovation Unit [awarded Rocket Lab a $32 million contract](https://defensescoop.com/2024/04/11/rocket-lab-true-anomaly-victus-haze-contracts/) for the VICTUS HAZE mission: a demonstration of tactically responsive space, requiring both spacecraft manufacture and launch of a Pioneer-class satellite aboard an Electron from New Zealand's Mahia Peninsula within twenty-four hours of a "go" order. The spacecraft would then demonstrate rendezvous and proximity operations against a simulated adversary asset. By March 2026, Rocket Lab had gone further still, securing a [four-year, $190 million block-buy contract](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-190m-contract-20x-haste-launches-cements) for twenty suborbital launches of HASTE — the Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron — under the Pentagon's MACH-TB 2.0 hypersonic test programme. At announcement the HASTE deal was the largest single launch contract in company history.

## Commercial Anchor Tenants: Synspective and Capella

Among commercial operators, the most durable anchor relationship was with the Japanese synthetic-aperture radar company Synspective. Rocket Lab had launched Synspective's first StriX demonstration satellite as early as 2020; by June 2024 the partnership had graduated to a formal multi-launch agreement. In September 2025, the two parties [struck a second block of ten dedicated Electron missions](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-and-synspective-strike-another-10-launch-deal-boosting-contracted-missions-to-21-electron-launches/), lifting the total contracted Synspective manifest to twenty-one launches — the single largest dedicated-mission order from any one customer in Electron's history — with launches scheduled through the end of the decade.

Capella Space, the San Francisco-based SAR operator, presented a structurally similar relationship. In early 2023 Rocket Lab signed a multi-launch deal to [deploy four dedicated Electron missions](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-signs-multi-launch-deal-to-deploy-satellite-constellation-for-capella-space/) carrying Capella's Acadia satellites into low Earth orbit, beginning in the second half of 2023, supplementing a prior mission already on the manifest. Both Synspective and Capella relied on Electron's dedicated-rideshare model — each mission flying a single satellite to a customer-specified orbital plane — which justified pricing premiums over shared-ride alternatives and contributed to the per-mission average selling price that management consistently cited in guidance.

## Globalstar: The Prime Spacecraft Manufacturer Test Case

The most consequential commercial spacecraft contract was assembled in two layers. In late 2022, Canadian satellite manufacturer MDA Space named Rocket Lab as the spacecraft bus supplier for Globalstar's next-generation low-Earth-orbit constellation, to be funded principally by Apple as part of its emergency satellite communications service. [Rocket Lab's share of the contract was $143 million](https://spacenews.com/globalstar-selects-mda-and-rocket-lab-for-new-satellites/), covering the design and manufacture of seventeen Lightning-platform spacecraft buses, with options for the satellite operations control centre, launch dispensers, and up to nine additional vehicles. MDA would act as prime contractor and handle payload integration.

The programme proved more demanding than the original schedule suggested. Production of the seventeen buses encountered delays that [pushed the first launch target](https://www.spaceintelreport.com/mda-rocket-labs-17-satellite-globalstar-contract-delayed-again-to-mid-2026-globalstar-to-impose-liquidated-damages/) into mid-2026 — a slip that attracted liquidated-damages clauses from Globalstar. The delays were an early test of Rocket Lab's ability to execute at spacecraft-prime scale; management attributed them to hardware and test complexity rather than design deficiencies, and maintained that production was on a revised path.

## Propellants, Feedstocks, and the Physics of the Stack

Electron's Rutherford engine burns RP-1 — highly refined, low-sulphur kerosene — against liquid oxygen. The choice was deliberate: RP-1 is a room-temperature propellant with well-understood handling characteristics, widely available from industrial gas suppliers, and storable at launch sites without the cryogenic infrastructure that liquid hydrogen demands. Liquid oxygen is drawn from commercial industrial-gas supply chains at both Mahia and Wallops. The relatively modest volumes required per Electron mission — the rocket stands just seventeen metres tall and lifts off at roughly 12,500 kilograms — meant that propellant procurement had remained a logistics variable rather than a strategic constraint through the Electron programme's first fifty-plus flights.

Neutron introduces a different chemistry. Rocket Lab's [Archimedes engine](https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2021/12/neutron-update-dec-2021/) burns liquid oxygen against liquid methane — the same propellant combination chosen by SpaceX for Raptor — in an oxidiser-rich staged-combustion cycle producing up to 165,000 pounds of thrust per engine. Nine Archimedes units will fire from Neutron's first stage at liftoff. Launch Complex 3 at Wallops, [formally opened in August 2025](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-a-critical-milestone-on-the-path-to-neutrons-first-launch/), was built around this propellant stack: the pad infrastructure includes 180,000-gallon cryogenic farms for both LOX and liquefied natural gas, the methane feedstock for Archimedes. The shift from kerosene to methane represents the single largest propellant-supply transition in Rocket Lab's operational history and will require LNG sourcing agreements of a scale well beyond Electron's RP-1 requirements.

## Components, Acquisitions, and the Manufacturing Footprint

The components supply chain is largely internal — the 2020–2022 acquisition arc created a vertically integrated stack of reaction wheels, flight software, Hall-effect thrusters, and solar cells that feeds both third-party customers and Rocket Lab's own Photon buses.

The physical anchor of the engine supply chain is the Long Beach Engine Development Center, opened in October 2023 in a 144,000-square-foot facility [acquired from Virgin Orbit's bankruptcy estate for $16.1 million](https://spacenews.com/rocket-lab-opens-engine-facility-in-former-virgin-orbit-headquarters/). CFO Adam Spice, at the opening, described the acquisition's principal benefit as "de-risking" the schedule for scaling engine production. The centre runs high-rate manufacturing of the 3D-printed Rutherford — Rocket Lab rolled its one-thousandth Rutherford off the line before the facility opened — and serves as the development and early-production site for Archimedes, with hot-fire testing conducted at NASA's Stennis Space Center in Mississippi. New Zealand contributes a complementary industrial layer: Auckland handles propellant-tank fabrication and Electron vehicle integration, while a carbon-composite facility in Warkworth, acquired from SailGP Technologies, supports both the growing Electron production rate and Neutron's composite-intensive airframe. The geographic split — critical engine technology onshored to Southern California, structural fabrication retained in New Zealand — reflected both the national-security sensitivities of the US government customer base and the cost economics of composite manufacturing in the Southern Hemisphere.

By the snapshot date, the aggregate order backlog had crossed $2.2 billion, a figure that captured launch commitments from Synspective, Capella, the confidential eight-launch Neutron-and-Electron deal announced in May 2026, and the Space Systems contracts for SDA and the Globalstar programme. The backlog, more than any single data point, illustrated how completely the company had moved beyond the early model of selling Electron seats one mission at a time.

---

**Sources referenced:** [NASA CAPSTONE contract](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-contract-to-launch-cubesat-to-moon-from-virginia/) · [SolAero acquisition](https://techcrunch.com/2022/01/18/rocket-lab-acquires-solaero-holdings-for-80m-to-boost-space-solar-cell-production/) · [CHIPS funding Albuquerque](https://www.nist.gov/chips/rocket-lab-new-mexico-albuquerque) · [SDA T2 $515M](https://defensescoop.com/2024/01/08/rocket-lab-sda-tranche-2-beta-award/) · [SDA T3 $816M](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-awarded-816m-prime-contract-to-build-missile-defense-satellite-constellation-for-u-s-space-force/) · [VICTUS HAZE $32M](https://defensescoop.com/2024/04/11/rocket-lab-true-anomaly-victus-haze-contracts/) · [HASTE $190M](https://investors.rocketlabcorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rocket-lab-secures-190m-contract-20x-haste-launches-cements) · [Synspective 21-launch deal](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-and-synspective-strike-another-10-launch-deal-boosting-contracted-missions-to-21-electron-launches/) · [Capella multi-launch](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-signs-multi-launch-deal-to-deploy-satellite-constellation-for-capella-space/) · [Globalstar/MDA $143M](https://spacenews.com/globalstar-selects-mda-and-rocket-lab-for-new-satellites/) · [Globalstar delays](https://www.spaceintelreport.com/mda-rocket-labs-17-satellite-globalstar-contract-delayed-again-to-mid-2026-globalstar-to-impose-liquidated-damages/) · [Neutron methane switch](https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2021/12/neutron-update-dec-2021/) · [LC3 opening](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-opens-launch-complex-3-a-critical-milestone-on-the-path-to-neutrons-first-launch/) · [Virgin Orbit facility](https://spacenews.com/rocket-lab-opens-engine-facility-in-former-virgin-orbit-headquarters/)

chapters.title: Where Rocket Lab sits against SpaceX, Firefly, Astra, and the broader launch landscape
chapters.body:
## The Field Narrows

When Rocket Lab founder and chief executive Peter Beck took Electron to its first successful orbit in January 2018, the small-launch market looked like it might support a dozen competitors. By the time of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, that field had been compressed by physics, capital markets, and operational reality into a handful of viable players — and Rocket Lab had emerged as the clear survivor in its weight class.

The story of the competitive landscape is, in one sense, a story of attrition. Virgin Orbit, Richard Branson's air-launched small rocket spinout, declared bankruptcy in April 2023 after a catastrophic mission failure over the UK in January of that year wiped out its remaining customer confidence and financing runway. ABL Space Systems, which had raised more than $200 million and won US Space Force contracts for its RS1 vehicle, quietly wound down operations in early 2023 after two consecutive launch failures left its manifest in tatters. Astra Space, which had gone public via SPAC in 2021 at a roughly $2.1 billion valuation and traded on Nasdaq under the ticker ASTR, formally abandoned its Rocket 4.0 medium-launch programme by mid-2023 and pivoted toward satellite propulsion systems — a retreat that left the company a fraction of its listed peak. The [SpaceX](https://www.spacex.com) thesis — that launch vehicles are extremely hard to build, and that incumbents with flight heritage would crush newcomers — proved correct at an accelerated pace.

## Small Launch: One Dominant Survivor

Against that backdrop, Electron sits largely alone at the operational end of the Western small-launch market. With more than fifty missions through 2025, Electron has accumulated a cadence and reliability record that no rival in its payload class has matched.

Firefly Aerospace, backed by AE Industrial Partners and operating from Vandenberg Space Force Base, has made the most credible effort to push into the small-to-medium gap. Its Alpha rocket — capable of lifting roughly 1,000 kilograms to LEO, roughly three times Electron's capacity — achieved its first successful orbital mission in October 2022 after a first-flight failure in 2021. The Victus Nox mission in September 2023, a US Space Force tactically responsive launch demonstration that saw Firefly prepare and fly Alpha within 24 hours of a call-up, was a genuine technical milestone and a pointed demonstration of the kind of government utility that the small-launch segment must provide to survive.

Firefly's trajectory is instructive for understanding where Rocket Lab's moat lies. Alpha's payload is larger, but its cadence through early 2026 remained well below Electron's, and Firefly had not yet demonstrated the kind of multi-launch per-year rhythm that commercial operators require for scheduling confidence. Rocket Lab, with a decade of launch operations across two continents and a proprietary launch site at Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand that provides orbital flexibility no rival outside SpaceX can match, had turned operational reliability into a competitive barrier that capital alone could not quickly replicate.

## Medium Launch: The Falcon 9 Problem

If the small-launch field belongs to Rocket Lab by default, the medium-launch arena presents the company's most consequential bet. Neutron is explicitly designed to address the commercial and government medium-lift market where SpaceX's Falcon 9 is deeply entrenched.

The Falcon 9's statistical record makes it the most operationally capable orbital launch vehicle ever built. Through 2025, SpaceX had conducted more than 300 Falcon 9 missions, achieving an orbital success rate that the industry had not previously thought achievable. The vehicle's reusable first stage had routinely returned for landing on drone ships after its ninth, tenth, and higher flights. More importantly for competitive analysis, SpaceX's manufacturing scale and vertical integration had driven per-kilogram launch costs to levels that made Falcon 9 the default choice for any operator that could tolerate its scheduling queue. List prices were rarely disclosed publicly, but market participants consistently described Falcon 9 pricing in the range of $67 million per launch for a dedicated mission — a number that competitors including Neutron would need to undercut or match on a cost-per-kilogram basis to win commercial business.

The competitive picture in medium launch beyond SpaceX is more complicated. United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur conducted its first launch in January 2024 carrying Astrobotic's Peregrine lunar lander and began certifying for national-security payloads. Blue Origin's New Glenn — a heavy-lift vehicle substantially larger than Neutron at roughly 45,000 kilograms to LEO in expendable configuration — achieved its first launch in January 2025 in what the company characterised as a partial success, reaching orbit but experiencing an anomaly with the upper stage. Arianespace's Ariane 6, long delayed, completed its inaugural flight in July 2024. None of these vehicles, as of May 2026, had approached the cadence or per-flight economics of Falcon 9.

| Vehicle | Payload to LEO (reusable) | Operator | Status (May 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Falcon 9 | ~17,400 kg | SpaceX | Fully operational; 300+ missions |
| New Glenn | ~45,000 kg (expendable) | Blue Origin | Early operational; limited cadence |
| Ariane 6 | ~21,600 kg | Arianespace | Operational; limited commercial cadence |
| Vulcan Centaur | ~27,200 kg | ULA | Operational; NSS certification in progress |
| **Neutron** | **~13,000 kg** | **Rocket Lab** | **In development; first launch slipping** |

Beck acknowledged the challenge on multiple occasions. In quarterly commentary through 2024 and 2025, he declined to provide firm first-launch dates as Neutron's development schedule slipped, focusing instead on the progress of its carbon composite structure and the Archimedes engine programme. The strategic logic remained intact: Neutron's reusable architecture is designed to deliver economics competitive with Falcon 9 at a scale that allows Rocket Lab to capture a meaningful share of constellation replenishment, government dedicated missions, and commercial operator demand that SpaceX's own internal Starlink programme cannot prioritise.

## Space Systems: Where the Primes Meet a Disruptor

Rocket Lab's Space Systems segment occupies a different competitive quadrant — one populated by Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman, and a shrinking cohort of pure-play satellite suppliers. Maxar Technologies, once the dominant commercial Earth-observation spacecraft manufacturer, was taken private by Advent International in a deal that closed in 2023 at approximately $6.4 billion, removing it from the listed-company comparison set. What remained in the public markets was a gap that Rocket Lab, through its acquisitions of Sinclair Interplanetary (reaction wheels, 2020), Advanced Solutions Inc. (attitude control software, 2021), SolAero Technologies (solar arrays, 2021), and Planetary Systems Corporation (separation systems, 2021), was systematically positioned to fill.

The competitive differentiation Beck articulated was vertical integration: a Photon customer sources reaction wheels, solar cells, propulsion, flight software, separation, and launch from a single vendor. No comparable offering exists at Rocket Lab's scale outside the large defence primes.

The government customer base added a strategic depth layer that pure commercial competitors lacked. Multiple US Space Force contracts for responsive launch and dedicated spacecraft programmes had been disclosed in annual and quarterly filings, providing recurring revenue that smoothed the inherent lumpiness of commercial launch manifests.

## The Integration Thesis Under Pressure

The competitive position Rocket Lab had constructed by May 2026 rested on a proposition that was simultaneously its greatest strength and its most exposed risk. Electron's flight heritage and operational superiority over its direct small-launch rivals gave the company a cash-generating base that no rival below SpaceX could match. Space Systems' component acquisition strategy had built genuine product depth. But Neutron — the vehicle on which the entire medium-launch competitive thesis depended — remained unflown, and the competitive window against a Falcon 9 that showed no signs of obsolescence was not open indefinitely.

> "We're not building Neutron to compete with where Falcon 9 is today," Beck said in one of his public addresses to investors. "We're building it to compete with where the market needs to go."

Whether the market moved fast enough to validate that calculation before capital patience ran out was the central question that the Neutron programme posed for the company's competitive positioning — and the one that sophisticated investors in the launch sector were watching most closely.

chapters.title: From 2018 Electron through 2021 SPAC, acquisitions, and Neutron development
chapters.body:
## Electron Finds Orbit

January 21, 2018: Rocket Lab's second Electron reached orbit from Māhia Peninsula, opening the commercial era. The first commercial mission — "It's Business Time" — followed in November 2018.

## Cadence, CAPSTONE, and the Run to Markets

The Photon platform — originally Electron's kick stage evolved into a standalone spacecraft bus — broadened the addressable market. NASA's selection of Photon for CAPSTONE validated deep-space applications. By 2021, the Neutron development thesis required capital beyond what private markets could efficiently support.

## The SPAC Combination

August 25, 2021: Rocket Lab completed its business combination with Vector Acquisition Corporation, listing on Nasdaq under ticker RKLB. Proceeds funded Electron scaling and Neutron's initial capitalisation. The public listing also provided acquisition currency for the Space Systems build-out.

## Assembling the Space Systems Segment

The acquisition arc ran through an eighteen-month window: Sinclair (April 2020), plasma propulsion (October 2021), ASI and Solero (December 2021). Together the acquisitions assembled components spanning power, propulsion, attitude control, and software — the subsystems Rocket Lab could bundle into Photon buses or sell standalone. By 2024, Space Systems contributed 70–75 percent of total revenue. See **Financial Deep Dive** for detailed segment breakouts.

## Neutron: Contesting the Medium Class

Neutron, announced March 2021, established a manufacturing facility in Middle River, Maryland. The vehicle incorporated a reusable first stage from inception. First-launch targets slipped from 2024–2025 toward 2026; as of the snapshot date, Neutron had not flown.

## Forward Catalysts

Three events define the investor calendar: (1) Neutron's first launch — the highest-magnitude catalyst, unlocking medium-lift contracts; (2) Space Systems margin expansion as acquired companies rationalise into coherent manufacturing; (3) Electron cadence sustainability, generating the revenue base and operational proof supporting Neutron's commercial credibility.

chapters.title: Electron, Neutron, Photon, and the Space Systems components IP
chapters.body:
## The Rutherford Engine and Electron's Composite Architecture

Rocket Lab's intellectual property empire begins, as most things in the company do, with an unconventional engineering decision. The Rutherford engine — nine of which power Electron's first stage, with a vacuum-optimised variant on the second — was the first flight-ready orbital engine ever to use an electric-pump-fed cycle. Where conventional rocket engines drive propellant pumps with turbines running off bleed gas or pre-burner exhaust, Rutherford deploys brushless DC electric motors spinning at 40,000 rpm, drawing from a lithium-polymer battery bank that exceeds one megawatt of combined output across all nine first-stage engines. [Rocket Lab claims](https://rocketlabcorp.com/updates/rocket-lab-celebrates-100th-rutherford-engine-build/) pump efficiency of roughly 95 percent, against approximately 50 percent for conventional gas-generator cycles.

The propellants are RP-1 and liquid oxygen — unremarkable choices — but the manufacturing process is not. All major Rutherford components, including the combustion chamber, injectors, propellant pumps and main valves, are produced via Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS), a 3D-printing process that reduces engine fabrication to roughly 24 hours per unit. Sea-level thrust stands at 24.9 kilonewtons with a specific impulse of 311 seconds; the vacuum Rutherford extends that to 343 seconds through a larger nozzle. The engine weighs 35 kilograms dry. By 2024, Rocket Lab had manufactured more than 1,000 Rutherfords — a production cadence that no small-launch competitor has matched.

Surrounding those engines is an equally proprietary airframe. Electron was the first orbital-class rocket to fly with carbon-fibre composite propellant tanks, a design that required developing entirely new manufacturing techniques for composite structures compatible with cryogenic liquid oxygen. A robotic production system nicknamed "Rosie the Robot" reduced composite part fabrication time from 400 hours to 12 hours per vehicle. Together, the Rutherford engine and composite architecture constitute a launch vehicle that cost roughly $7.5 million per flight to customers — a price point that enabled commercial small-satellite operators to buy dedicated rideshare access without pooling payloads.

Rocket Lab pursued booster recovery to defend that price point at scale. After successful ocean splashdowns beginning with the November 2020 "Return to Sender" mission, it achieved the world's first mid-air helicopter catch of a rocket booster in May 2022. The programme was subsequently wound down in favour of ocean splashdown recovery, with the emphasis shifting to re-qualifying and reflying Rutherford engines rather than full-stage refurbishment.

## Neutron and the Archimedes Engine

Neutron is where Rocket Lab's IP ambition scales by an order of magnitude. The medium lift vehicle — 42.8 metres tall, 480,000 kilograms at liftoff, targeting 13,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit in reusable configuration and 15,000 kilograms expendable — is powered by nine Archimedes engines, each generating 730 kilonewtons at sea level and 890 kilonewtons in vacuum, at 329 and 365 seconds specific impulse respectively, burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen.

The Archimedes design underwent a significant internal pivot. When Rocket Lab first publicly detailed Neutron in late 2021, the engine was specified as a gas-generator cycle. By September 2022, Beck had switched to oxidizer-rich staged combustion — the thermodynamically superior cycle that extracts more energy from propellants before combustion. The rationale was propulsive reusability: achieving the throttle range and turbine temperature margins needed to land a heavy booster repeatedly required the cycle change. "Neutron is an entirely new kind of rocket," Beck stated in late 2025 commentary, "and it's been developed on a really, really rapid timeline to meet the demand for our constellation customers, and of course, high assurance missions for the nation." A full mission-duration hot-fire of Archimedes was completed at NASA Stennis Space Center in August 2025.

Neutron's most distinctive structural feature is its payload fairing, which Rocket Lab has branded the "Hungry Hippo." Unlike conventional fairings that are jettisoned and lost, Neutron's fairing halves are hinged to the first stage; they open at staging, the upper stage departs, and the fairings snap shut again around the first stage in under 1.5 seconds before re-entry. The qualification campaign concluded in December 2025, with the fairing shipped to Launch Complex 3 at Wallops Island, Virginia.

Development has not been without setbacks. A first-stage propellant tank ruptured during hydrostatic pressure testing at Rocket Lab's Maryland facility in January 2026. Beck acknowledged the failure publicly, attributing it to a manufacturing defect and committing to a revised qualification campaign. First launch remains targeted for late 2026 — a programme that has slipped roughly two years from its original 2024 estimate, though hardware milestones have continued to accumulate.

## Photon and the Spacecraft Platform

The Photon spacecraft bus began life as Electron's kick stage and was progressively developed into a full-service satellite platform. Propulsion comes from the Curie engine — a 3D-printed, restartable, pressure-fed thruster whose propellant chemistry Rocket Lab treats as a trade secret — and the more powerful HyperCurie, an electric-pump-fed variant used on deep-space missions. The [CAPSTONE mission for NASA](https://rocketlabcorp.com/missions/missions-launched/capstone/) in 2022 demonstrated Photon's interplanetary capability through trans-lunar injection. Photon's next deep-space demonstration, the twin-spacecraft ESCAPADE Mars magnetosphere mission, launched aboard New Glenn in November 2025 and remains in transit toward Mars orbit insertion in September 2027.

## Space Systems: The Acquired Components Stack

The 2020–2022 acquisition arc assembled a vertically integrated supply chain. SolAero is arguably the most strategically scarce: one of only two US producers of high-efficiency space-grade multi-junction solar cells, covering more than 1,000 successful space missions. Its IMM-beta cell, at 33.3 percent beginning-of-life efficiency, represents the leading commercial product in its class.
