Planetary Systems' Motorized Lightband — 100-plus on-orbit separations with claimed 100 percent success — controls a critical deployment bottleneck.

## R&D Investment Against Revenue

R&D outlays rose from $41.8 million (FY2021) to $174.4 million (FY2024) — a 317 percent increase.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | R&D Expense | R&D / Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | $62.2M | $41.8M | 67% |
| 2022 | $211.0M | $65.2M | 31% |
| 2023 | $244.6M | $119.1M | 49% |
| 2024 | $436.2M | $174.4M | 40% |

*Sources: [FY2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819994/000162828025008724/rklb-20241231.htm), [FY2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001819994/000095017024022160/rklb-20231231.htm)*

The SEC filings attribute virtually all incremental R&D growth to Neutron — personnel, prototype hardware, Archimedes test articles — with secondary contributions from spacecraft components product-line expansion. The fiscal 2023 jump of 83 percent year-on-year reflected the acceleration of Archimedes engine development; the further 46 percent increase in 2024 reflected Neutron structural hardware and launch site preparation. A company with $174 million of annual R&D on $436 million of revenue is, by any conventional measure, still primarily in investment mode. The question embedded in that ratio is whether Neutron's first launch, whenever it occurs, begins to amortise that spend across a manifest large enough to justify it.

chapters.title: Neutron development risk, SpaceX competition, capex intensity, customer concentration
chapters.body:
## Neutron: Schedule Risk and the Burden of Reusability

The central investment risk was architectural. The company was attempting to build, certify, and commercially operate a reusable medium-lift vehicle while sustaining Electron operations and expanding Space Systems. Neutron's development timeline became a primary variable in every investor model.

Slippages accumulated: from 2024 to late 2025 to 2026. Neutron's architecture demands propulsive return-to-launch-site, a substantially harder regime than Electron's helicopter recovery. SpaceX's mastery of that capability took years and multiple vehicle losses. Until reusability is validated at scale, Neutron's unit economics remain theoretical.

## The SpaceX Problem

SpaceX's Falcon 9 had accumulated over 200 consecutive successful missions by 2025, with captive Starlink demand spreading fixed costs across volume that external competitors cannot replicate. Neutron's commercial proposition rests on schedule availability, dedicated-mission economics, and government preference for supply-chain diversity. The risk: that utility may not translate into sufficient volume to sustain programme economics against Falcon 9 dominance.

## Capex Intensity and the Path to Profitability

The company simultaneously funded three demands: Electron operations, Space Systems expansion, and Neutron development. The forward draw on capital — engine qualification, vehicle integration, Wallops infrastructure, potential test failures — was a known uncertainty. Programmes of this complexity routinely exceed initial budgets; material overruns would require capital market access at terms determined by prevailing sentiment toward pre-revenue space infrastructure companies.

## Government Customer Concentration

The composition of Rocket Lab's customer base introduced a specific concentration risk that sophisticated investors in the space sector recognised from prior cycles. NASA and the US Department of Defense — including Space Force programmes — represented a material and growing share of the company's backlog. Photon spacecraft had flown NASA's CAPSTONE lunar mission; multiple Space Force contracts had been disclosed through the snapshot period; Electron's launch manifest included significant government content.

Government customers confer advantages but introduce vulnerabilities: appropriations cycles, continuing resolutions, and programme restructurings can disrupt schedules. Concentration limits negotiating leverage — programme-dependent revenue requires relationship continuity with a small number of bureaucratic decision-makers.

## Launch Failure Risk

Electron's 50-plus mission record was not without incident; early failures contributed to insurance market pricing across the sector. For Neutron, the failure risk is starker: a first-flight failure would reset the commercial timeline by 12–18 months and consume additional capital. Multiple early failures would call into question whether the programme could be completed within a commercially viable cost envelope.

## Space Industry Cyclicality

The satellite and space infrastructure investment cycle introduced a macro risk that sat beneath the company-specific factors. Constellation buildouts — the primary driver of demand for both small and medium lift — were financed by venture and institutional capital that moved with risk appetite. When funding cycles contracted, constellation programmes deferred launches, reduced planned scale, or failed outright, compressing launch manifest and space systems procurement simultaneously. The 2022–2023 period had demonstrated this dynamic across the broader new space sector, with several constellation operators facing financing pressure and revised deployment schedules. Rocket Lab's diversified customer base and government exposure provided partial insulation, but the company was not immune to a sustained contraction in commercial satellite investment. In a sector where Rocket Lab was building a new vehicle for a market partly defined by future constellation demand, the cyclicality risk was an underwriting uncertainty that no degree of technical execution could fully hedge.

chapters.title: Neutron first launch, Space Systems scaling, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## Neutron: the medium-lift wager

The thesis that elevated Rocket Lab beyond a launch-services vendor rests on a single unproven rocket. As of late May 2026, Neutron had slipped past the late-2025 target window, making the development schedule the principal variable investors were pricing into the stock.

The architecture reflected deliberate choices: nine in-house Archimedes engines, recoverable first stage via "latch and catch" at the launch mount (rather than sea-landing), expendable second stage, carbon-composite structures throughout. Launch Complex 3 at Wallops represented the single largest capital allocation in Rocket Lab's post-SPAC history.

Neutron's revenue contribution is transformational, not incremental. Electron's sub-350-kilogram class is commercially relevant but bounded; Neutron addresses the multi-ton class driving constellation replenishment, national security launches, and deep-space opportunities.

## Space Systems: the scaling engine

By 2024, Space Systems contributed 70–75 percent of total revenue. Photon had matured from an Electron upper-stage derivative into a standalone spacecraft bus with interplanetary credentials. Government customer breadth expanded materially through 2023–2025 — US Space Force contracts signalled clearance of national-security vetting thresholds. Commercial operators including Synspective, Capella Space, and Globalstar diversified the revenue base away from single-mission dependence.

## Risks the ledger still carries

Operating losses remained substantial through 2023. Neutron's case rests on the premise that customers will value mission-dedicated medium launches on a non-SpaceX vehicle — premises reasonable but not guaranteed to generate sufficient demand density.

Electron's competitive position faced evolution: Firefly Alpha demonstrated success; European vendors advanced toward operational status. The small-launch market was becoming multi-vendor.

Neutron's reusability execution — recovering first stage at the launch mount — had no direct Western operational precedent. The engineering rationale was sound; the execution track record did not yet exist.

## The central question

The 2026–2030 horizon for Rocket Lab resolves, ultimately, into two separable but interconnected questions. First: can Neutron achieve a successful first launch and then — critically — operational cadence at economics that sustain the programme? Second: can the Space Systems segment continue scaling organically, deepening customer relationships across both commercial and national-security channels, in a way that produces improving operating margins even before Neutron contributes a single kilogram of paid payload?

The Space Systems answer, while not certain, was the more tractable of the two as of May 2026. The segment had demonstrated consistent revenue growth, customer diversification, and the beginnings of vertical integration economics through the Photon platform. Beck had built a components-and-spacecraft business that would carry strategic value even in a scenario where Neutron encountered further delay.

Neutron was the harder question, because its answer was binary in a way that Space Systems was not. A Neutron that launches and demonstrates reusability on schedule transforms Rocket Lab's revenue profile, its addressable market, and its competitive positioning relative to every Western launch provider except SpaceX. A Neutron that encounters further material slippage, or that struggles to achieve the reuse economics its architecture assumes, leaves the company in an asymmetric position: a mature small-launch franchise attached to an expensive development programme drawing down cash at scale. The dossier's reader, constructing a view on RKLB across the five-year horizon, was ultimately making a judgment about which of those two outcomes Rocket Lab's engineering organisation — and Peter Beck's record of delivering rockets that were supposed to be impossible to build — made more probable.
